audit: initialize accepts a user‑supplied options[:cluster] array of node addresses (strings or hashes), parses them via URI, and then uses the resulting host/port to establish TCP connections. An attacker controlling these parameters can force the client to connect to arbitrary internal or external hosts (SSRF).
params: options[:cluster] → Option#parse_node_url / Option#parse_node_option → Node#build_clients → Client#connect (socket connect via establish_connection)

audit: process takes an arbitrary commands array and dispatches each command to the Redis server via Client#write over the network without sanitization. An attacker controlling these command arguments (e.g. EVAL scripts) can execute arbitrary code on the remote Redis instance, leading to RCE.
params: commands → Redis::Cluster#process → Node#process_all / assign_node + try_send → Client#process → Client#write → connection.write (Redis server execution)

audit: get_diagram_uri blindly concatenates the supplied server_url, the diagram type, format, the Base64‑style encoded diagram text, and any opts into a single HTTP URI via _join_uri_segments and opts.map for query parameters. There is no whitelisting or validation of server_url, type or format beyond trimming leading/trailing slashes, nor sanitization of interior “../” path segments, allowing an attacker to craft internal URLs or path‑traversal URIs that will be fetched by KrokiHttpClient, leading to SSRF.

InputStream.open takes an untrusted context parameter that flows directly into get_io, which calls ::File.open for string inputs or dup/seek for IO objects, enabling arbitrary local file reads if an attacker controls the path. The optional decrypter parameter is then used via header_bytesize and reset! calls on the supplied object, allowing execution of arbitrary code in a user‑provided decrypter. Neither context nor decrypter inputs are sanitized or constrained.

HTTParty.get forwards the user-controlled URL path directly through URI.parse into an unrestrictive Net::HTTP request chain, allowing SSRF. The ssl_ca_file and ssl_ca_path options flow into SSL certificate setup and will read arbitrary files for validation. The default XML parser uses MultiXml.parse (via Parser#xml), which may enable XXE-based file disclosure. Procs passed via query_string_normalizer, parser, or connection_adapter options are invoked at runtime, enabling arbitrary code execution if untrusted input is used.
Stores an :extract_access_token Proc in options for later invocation (RCE risk) and accepts a :site option that ultimately controls the HTTP request host (SSRF risk) for all subsequent requests.
The site= setter controls the base host passed to Faraday.new; if this value is attacker‑controlled, it enables SSRF on all HTTP requests made via the client.

get_token passes user‑supplied params directly into an HTTP request body or query string, enabling SSRF if the endpoint host is attacker‑controlled, and also invokes an extract_access_token Proc (if provided via argument or options), leading to arbitrary code execution in the legacy token‑parsing path.
Executes HTTP calls via Faraday.run_request on the provided URL and opts[:params]/opts[:body], allowing SSRF if these inputs or the Location header (redirects) are attacker‑controlled.

The create method blindly accepts arbitrary URI strings or hashes via its `*options` parameter and routes them through `extract_addresses_and_options`, which in turn uses `resolve` to map them to host/socket configurations. No validation or allow‑listing is performed before handing off to the Redis client, allowing an attacker to trigger network (TCP) or UNIX‐socket connections to attacker‑controlled endpoints. This uncontrolled host/path injection constitutes a classic SSRF risk.

This method directly feeds user‑provided URIs into `URI.parse` and then copies the resulting scheme, host, port, path, user/password (via `CGI.unescape`), and any query parameters (via `URI.decode_www_form`) straight into the Redis client options hash. No sanitization or restriction is applied to the target host, port, or UNIX‐socket path, enabling arbitrary SSRF to remote services or local UNIX sockets. The query decoding even allows control over additional client options, widening the attack surface.

params.uri: URI.parse → CGI.unescape(uri.password) → URI.decode_www_form(uri.query) → direct mapping into client options

audit: Initialize stores a user‑supplied directory URL (and connection_options) which is later used by HTTPClient to perform requests. This enables SSRF (and proxy/redirect manipulation) via the directory or connection_options arguments.

The directory method invokes fetch_directory, which does a Faraday GET against @directory_url (set from user input in initialize). An attacker can supply any HTTP/HTTPS endpoint in the directory parameter and cause arbitrary SSRF.

The initializer unsafely forwards arbitrary options to the STS client constructor (including endpoint/http_proxy) and also accepts a before_refresh Proc which it will invoke, and allows a custom client object, enabling SSRF via user‑controlled endpoints or proxies and RCE via a malicious before_refresh or injected client.
params: before_refresh -> invoked in RefreshingCredentials#initialize and #refresh (arbitrary code execution)
client -> used in RefreshingCredentials#refresh via @client.assume_role (arbitrary method execution)
endpoint -> passed to STS::Client.new and used in HTTP call in #refresh (SSRF)
http_proxy -> passed to STS::Client.new and used in HTTP call in #refresh (SSRF)

audit: The method loads untrusted JSON controlling token_url, credential_source subfields, and service_account_impersonation_url, which feed directly into HTTP requests, file reads, and subprocess execution. Arbitrary token_url and service_account_impersonation_url lead to SSRF via STSClient.exchange_token and BaseCredentials#get_impersonated_access_token. Credential_source.url/file/executable drive SSRF in IdentityPool and AwsCredentials, file reads in IdentityPool and PluggableAuthCredentials, and command execution in PluggableAuthCredentials.
params: credential_source[:url] -> connection.get in IdentityPoolCredentials#url_data and AwsCredentials#fetch_metadata_role_name
subject_token_type -> conditional branch to AWS vs IdentityPool/Pluggable paths

audit: The initializer merges untrusted config and environment inputs then calls parse_config_file and parse_environment_variables without sanitization. It uses IO.foreach on a user‑supplied config_file path (arbitrary file read), eval on ENV['RES_OPTIONS'] (arbitrary code execution), and a nameservers setter that can trigger DNS lookups via nameservers_from_name → Resolver.search (SSRF).
params: config[:nameservers] → nameservers= → nameservers_from_name → Resolver.search → network calls

audit: The class method start(name, type, cls) calls new.search(name, type, cls), which flows the name and type directly into packet creation and send_tcp/send_udp socket calls. Unsanitized names result in arbitrary DNS queries (SSRF), and AXFR record types force TCP zone transfers.

The `path_or_url` argument is used without validation to drive either `URI.open` (for remote URLs) or `Pathname.open` (for local paths), enabling SSRF or arbitrary filesystem reads. That IO stream is then fed into `IO.copy_stream` into a tempfile, exfiltrating remote or local file contents under attacker control. The optional `ext` parameter merely sets the tempfile’s extension and does not sanitize the source. Subsequent validation via an external `identify` command does not mitigate the initial leakage.

construct hands the raw filter string directly to FilterParser.parse without sanitization, allowing attacker-controlled syntax to create arbitrary LDAP filters and inject clauses. There is no escaping or validation beyond grammar, leading to LDAP injection and unauthorized directory queries. No SSRF, RCE or file I/O are performed by this method.

eq builds a filter node with the attribute and raw value parameters without any escaping, so user-supplied wildcards or parentheses can alter filter logic and inject additional clauses. This leads to LDAP injection and potential unauthorized data exposure when the filter is used. No SSRF, RCE or file operations occur in this path.

ex constructs an extensible match filter node with the raw attribute and value parameters without escaping special characters, enabling LDAP injection via wildcard or syntax injection in the value. No SSRF, RCE or file I/O occur here, but unsanitized input can manipulate the filter semantics.

FilterParser.parse uses StringScanner and regular expressions to interpret the provided filter string and build a filter AST without sanitizing content, allowing any valid LDAP filter syntax from input to influence the tree. This directly enables LDAP injection if the input is attacker-controlled. No SSRF, RCE or file operations are performed.

The class‑method .open (and its instance open) take user‑supplied host/hosts parameters unfiltered and establish a TCPSocket, enabling SSRF if host is attacker‑controlled. In addition, encryption[:tls_options] is passed directly to OpenSSL::SSLContext#set_params, allowing arbitrary file reads (e.g. ca_file or cert paths) from the filesystem.

params.encryption[:tls_options][:cert]: similarly passed to SSLContext#set_params → certificate file read【F:lib/net/ldap.rb†L483-L533】【F:lib/net/ldap/connection.rb†L89-L96】

audit: Alias for Asciidoctor.convert, so it inherits the same SSRF, file-read/write, and RCE vectors as Asciidoctor.convert.
Alias for Asciidoctor.convert_file, so it inherits the same SSRF, file-read/write, and RCE vectors as Asciidoctor.convert_file.

Asciidoctor.convert merges user-supplied options and paths, then loads and parses the document with Document.load, which processes include directives and can read local or HTTP resources (SSRF/file-read) when safe mode is below Secure. It writes the converted output, stylesheets, and assets to disk based on options[:to_file], options[:to_dir], and mkdirs flags (file-write), and copies user-specified stylesheets via doc.read_asset and File.write (file-read/write). Custom template directories via the 'templatesdir' document attribute are normalized and scanned by TemplateConverter, which uses Tilt to load and ERB-render attacker-controlled templates (RCE).
params: input -> load -> Document.parse -> include:: processor -> File.open/OpenURI.open_uri
options[:to_dir] -> convert logic -> doc.normalize_system_path & Helpers.mkdir_p -> doc.write

audit: Asciidoctor.convert_file opens the user-specified filename for reading without restriction and delegates to Asciidoctor.convert, inheriting all include-based SSRF/file-read, output file-write, and template-driven RCE vulnerabilities when safe mode is below Secure.
params: all params of Asciidoctor.convert (to_file, to_dir, mkdirs, attributes templatesdir, stylesheet, copycss, stylesdir)
